speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES- PAYMENTS AT AGE 65
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 395, to provide for old age assistance.	_
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill now under consideration is part of Canada's new program for old age security, climaxing a quarter-century of progress in this field.
The government's twofold plan for old age assistance and universal pensions represents the greatest single advance made in this country in our provisions for senior Canadians. It is a national vote of confidence in Canada's capacity to provide for the security of its older citizens.

Legislation will be introduced in parliament in the fall session, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has indicated, to provide universal pensions at 70 years. This present old age assistance bill makes provision for those in the 65-69 age group who are in need of aid, as well as for those 70 years and over who cannot qualify for the universal pension. In a separate measure, also to be considered this session, allowances for the blind will be continued with certain relaxations in the ceilings on income.
The full implications of this program may not yet be fully realized. Let me remind the house of its broad outlines when it is fully in effect:
Old age assistance will be provided for an estimated one-third of those in the 65-69 age group, or about 145,000 persons.
Universal pensions of $40 a month will be paid to 715,000 Canadians of 70 and over, including 305,000 who are now receiving old age pensions.
In the first year a total of 860,000 Canadians, starting at age 65 will benefit under this new old age security program, which will cost about $410 million a year.
Since the first Old Age Pensions Act of 1927, our provision for old age security has been revised on several occasions. Twice during, the past four years it has been my privilege, as a member of this government, to introduce improved and expanded legislation to provide added security for our aged and blind citizens. As a result of these improvements, which have more than doubled the costs of pensions to the federal and provincial governments in this period: the total number of aged and blind pensioners has increased by nearly 100,000 to 313,371 at March 31, 1951; the basic statutory rate for pensions has been doubled-rising from $20 to $40; the income and residence requirements have been substantially liberalized; the citizenship requirement has been eliminated; the age of eligibility for blind pensioners has been reduced from 40 to 21; many provisions of the regulations have been improved.
In these past four years almost as much has been done to improve old age and blind pensions as in the preceding twenty. In addition, since 1949, pensioners have been paid in every province and territory of Canada.
While substantial progress has been made in recent years there was, however, no question that more could be done to improve our pensions program. But consideration had to be given to matters of constitutional responsibility as well as to matters involving financial limitations.
Old Age Assistance Act
That is why the federal government asked parliament last year to set up a special joint committee on old age security. Careful consideration was given by this committee to all aspects of the problem, including the burden resting on the provincial governments.
Since its proposals of 1945 to the provinces, the federal government had consistently favoured an old age security program consisting of old age assistance of up to $30 at 65, and universal pensions of $30 at 70.
The parliamentary committee, an all-party group, while recommending a higher basic pension than the 1945 proposals, otherwise confirmed this view in paragraph 51 on page 108 of its report:
51. All things considered, therefore, the committee is of the opinion that the most suitable old age security plan for Canada under present circumstances consists of a twofold program as follows:
(a)	A universal pay-as-you-go program applicable to all persons 70 years of age and over, based on the contributory principle and administered by the federal government. The benefit should be a flat, uniform amount of $40 a month for all eligible persons, and eligibility should be based solely on age and a suitable residence qualification.
(b)	For the age group 65 and over not eligible for the universal benefit, old age assistance at the rate of $40 a month should be available, subject to an eligibility test in some respects similar to that which exists under the present old age assistance program, but modified to take account of the different characteristics of the age group to which this test is to apply, and adjusted in such a way as to recognize to a greater extent than at present the desirability of encouraging recipients to earn supplemental income.
At the federal-provincial conference in December, 1950, the Prime Minister announced that these proposals were generally acceptable to the government. He said that the universal pension would be proceeded with as soon as there was unanimous agreement from the provinces on the constitutional amendment required.
The provinces all indicated their agreement with the federal program outlined, and subsequently approved the amendment enabling the federal government to establish a contributory system of pensions.
In May of this year, substantial agreement was also reached with all the provinces on the provisions to be made for the 65-69 group. This present measure reflects that agreement in every respect, and goes beyond it.
The universal pension will be paid from January of next year. When parliament has enacted the measure now before it, old age assistance will also be paid at the same time, if the provinces then pass similar legislation to take advantage of the federal offer.
Since the provinces will be relieved of the cost of pensions at 70 and over-of which they were paying one-quarter, and the federal government three-quarters of the basic

Old Age Assistance Act $40 pension-in sharing equally with the federal government the cost of old age assistance at 65, their costs will be no greater than at present.
The present measure for old age assistance is a natural extension of the 1945 proposals of the federal government; it was part of the twofold recommendation of the joint parliamentary committee; it is an integral part of that ideal old age security program of which I spoke to this house on March 10 of last year, as follows:
What we wish to do is to develop, within the limits only of the financial capacity of our people and with due regard to our over-all commitments in all fields of social security and other governmental responsibilities, the simplest, most effective and most humane system of old age security that it is possible for us to devise.
We wish to do this not in open disregard of provincial rights or interests or concerns, but in full consultation, agreement and partnership with the provinces.
I am sure that on examination of the bill now before the house, all members will agree that it implements fully the recommendations of the parliamentary committee with respect to the 65 to 69 age group, with the single exception that the residence qualification, instead of being fifteen years, is placed at twenty years, for reasons which I shall outline later when we deal with the matter in committee.
The present measure introduces for the first time the expression "old age assistance", in conformity with the committee's recommendations. The term "pension" will henceforth be reserved for the universal payments to those over 70, thus maintaining a clear distinction between the two types of payments to aged persons.
As the members of this house know, the sharing of costs with the provinces on a fifty-fifty basis, the age of eligibility at 65 and the $40 maximum amount of pension, are all in accordance with the recommendations of the joint parliamentary committee.
These provisions also meet the wishes of the provinces generally, as expressed at our meeting with them on May 23 and 24 last.
In deciding the payments to those between 65 and 69 on a selective basis, the government accepts the view of the parliamentary committee that the universal pension should not be applied to this group. There are several reason for this decision:
1.	It would involve an additional expenditure of $152 million in the first year alone.
2.	The number in this age group can be expected to increase at a greater rate than the entire population. If universal pensions were paid at 65, the cost by 1971 would amount to $782 million annually.


3.	The needs of the two groups are entirely different, since a great number of those between 65 and 69 are still actively engaged in productive employment, while the great majority of those 70 and over are retired.
4.	Payment of a universal pension at 65 would tend to encourage premature retirement at a time when a full labour force is needed in the national interest.
5.	The people of Canada are not prepared at this time, with other priorities of unmet need, to divert such a substantial proportion of the national income to old age security purposes.
6.	Finally, the provinces, who are required to participate in the program for the 65-69 age group on a fifty-fifty basis, feel the need of retaining some form of eligibility test.
The income ceilings in the bill before the house, which conform with the recommendations of the parliamentary committee, are more generous than those in the present Old Age Pensions Act.
The total allowable income, including old age assistance, has been increased as follows:
-for a single person, from $600 to $720;
-for a married couple, from $1,080 to
$1,200;
-for a married couple, with one blind spouse, from $1,200 to $1,320.
These adjustments recognize the desirability of encouraging those receiving old age assistance to earn supplemental income.
Here the government has gone beyond the recommendations of the committee in permitting the receipt of additional amounts, not only in earnings but in respect to income from other sources as well.
The question of income ceilings was fully discussed with the provinces at our conference last month. No province indicated a strong desire to set the ceilings any higher than those in the present bill. The majority of the provinces felt that the ceilings in the present Old Age Pensions Act were high enough.
The federal government has decided that in order to give each province the opportunity to decide for itself the limits of its generosity in this respect, the maximum should be set high enough to permit each province to go as far as it feels prepared to go.
While some provinces have indicated that these income ceilings might be too high, others have some doubts as to the advisability of commencing payment at as early an age as 65. Still others wish to set additional conditions of eligibility.
The federal government feels that, within the limits of administrative feasibility, each

province should be given the greatest possible leeway in establishing requirements to meet its particular capacities and needs.
Section 7 of this bill therefore makes it possible for each province, in its agreement with the federal government, to make its own provisions-within the framework of the federal measure-for the following: the maximum amount of assistance; the income ceilings; the minimum age; any special conditions of eligibility.
The federal government, of course-and this I underline-hopes, both for administrative reasons and on grounds of equity, that all provinces will ultimately adopt a uniform pattern in order to take the fullest advantage of the scope of this federal legislation.
In the meantime, it is not the intention of the government to insist on imposing this new program on all provinces on a "take it or leave it" basis. As the Prime Minister pointed out when he discussed this matter at the December conference with the provinces, it will be for each province to decide in the light of its own circumstances whether or not it will accept the offer contained in the federal legislation. None the less, if any province comes to the conclusion that it cannot, for reasons of its own, implement this part of the program in its jurisdiction at the present time, or that it can do so only on a limited and partial basis, this will not affect the federal government's offer as it applies to the other provinces. Nor will it in any way affect the implementation of the universal pension program.
I have dealt with the main features of the new legislation as they relate to the age of eligibility, the amount of assistance, the division of costs, and the income ceilings. Let me now mention a number of special changes which are necessary to note in order to appreciate the comprehensive scope of this bill.
Serious criticism has been made of the provision, which has been in the Old Age Pensions Act since 1927, for recovery from the estates of deceased pensioners. I now wish to announce that the government has decided to eliminate this requirement from this old age assistance measure.
This provision has always given rise to much misunderstanding. The thinking behind it was that if a pensioner left a substantial estate, it should benefit the taxpayer who had provided him with pension rather than someone who had shown little interest in the pensioner during his lifetime.
In actual fact, the total amounts recovered have never been great and have seldom
Old Age Assistance Act exceeded one-half of one per cent of pensions paid. In some provinces, either because of the more vigorous efforts of provincial pension authorities, or because persons with substantial means found their way on to the pension rolls, the amounts recovered have been greater than in other provinces.
In view of all this, the advisability of keeping this provision in the new bill was carefully weighed. It was decided that circumstances now will be considerably different from those under the old act where pensioners would remain on pension until death.
Under the new act, most persons receiving old age assistance will reach the age of 70 and transfer to the new universal pension, passing beyond the control of the provincial old age assistance authorities. The recovery provision is therefore no longer practical except for those who die between the ages of 65 and 69.
Some provinces, however, may still wish to continue this recovery practice under authority of their own legislation. The federal government cannot prevent this, but it is provided under section 7(d) that if a province does make such recoveries under its own authority, it must refund to the federal treasury half of all recoveries made, and the reason for that of course will be obvious.
Under section 10 of the Old Age Pensions Act, a province cannot be reimbursed by the federal government for any pension covering that portion of the month following the pensioner's death. This provision has always been unsatisfactory. Section 5, subsection 2, of this new legislation permits the province to be reimbursed: by the federal government if it pays a full pension for the month during which the recipient dies.
One additional feature of the new bill that I should like to emphasize is that it makes no special exclusion of Indians. In this bill, our native population is treated on a basis of complete equality with all other residents of Canada.
As most hon. members know, the present Old Age Pensions Act excludes from its benefits persons who are defined as Indians under the Indian Act. The federal government has for some years sought to remove this barrier against those who have a claim to being the first citizens of this country. This clause has remained in the act largely because of the wishes of the provinces, but I am now happy to say that, at our recent conference, the provinces generally agreed to our suggestion that Indians be placed on the same footing as others.

Old Age Assistance Act I am confident that experience will bear out the equity and justice of extending to our native population the benefits of this new forward step in our social security program.
I have now covered the main provisions of this old age assistance bill. I should add, however, that, unlike the Old Age Pensions Act, this bill makes no provision for the blind. This will be done in separate legislation to be introduced later this day, and to be known as the Blind Persons Act.
I shall reserve for the discussion of that bill any comments I may wish to make on the reasons why we have decided to separate the provisions relating to the blind' from the main provisions of the present bill relating to our older citizens.
The house will, for the present, I think, be satisfied to know that the new act will make full provision for the continuation of assistance to our blind citizens, and every safeguard will be employed to ensure that there is no interruption in payments during the transition from one act to another.
There are a number of other significant changes in terminology in the present measure, but I think these can be left to the detailed discussion which will take place in committee.
Section 7 of this bill relates to the form of agreement with the provinces. As hon. members are aware, legislation of this kind requires not only enabling legislation on the part of the provinces, but an agreement signed by the provincial and federal authorities.
Several sections scattered throughout the present Old Age Pensions Act deal with matters to be included in these agreements. From the point of view of orderly drafting, we have brought together all these points in this section 7.
At the time the parliamentary committee studied the costs of providing old age security, it estimated the probable costs of an old age assistance program of the kind set out in this bill. With little exact knowledge as to the nature of the eligibility test which might be included, and with no precise means for determining how many persons in the age group concerned might come under the legislation, the committee estimated the probable cost to be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $64 million yearly. On further consideration, these estimates still seem to be accurate.
On the fifty-fifty basis proposed in this legislation, and using these estimates, this would mean an annual expenditure of $32 million by the ten provinces and an equal expenditure by the federal government.
We know that the number of persons between the ages of 65 and 69 is substantially


lower than the number of those 70 and over, and that more of the younger group are actively employed and self-supporting. We therefore expect that the numbers qualifying for old age assistance will not exceed one-third of the total number of persons in Canada between the ages of 65 and 69.
If this estimate proves to be correct, it will mean that approximately 145,000 persons will receive old age assistance during the first year of operation of the new act. Since some provinces may decide on a higher minimum age, lower income ceilings or special conditions of eligibility, the actual numbers may not reach this estimate, although we hope, as I said earlier, that a uniform practice will be adopted throughout the country.
The federal share of the cost of the program will come from the consolidated revenue fund and not from the fund to be created for the financing of universal pensions, which will have from the start a contributory feature.
The provincial share will not represent an additional expenditure but simply a transfer out of the savings to the provinces when the federal government in January next relieves them of the cost of the provincial share of pensions payments now being made by them to those in the 70 and over group. In no case do we expect the provincial share to be greater than the cost they would incur next year if the Old Age Pensions Act were continued in its present form. In most cases provincial expenditures should be somewhat less than the savings which will result from federal assumption of pension payments to those persons 70 years of age and over.
In my opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, I spoke of this old age assistance measure as one part of Canada's new program for old age security. The all-party parliamentary committee, in adopting this program, gave unanimous support to it, which was a remarkable tribute both to the soundness of the government's plan and to the impartiality of the members of the committee in this vital field of human welfare. I now want to say to the chairman and every member of that committee, representing every political party in this house, that parliament and the country will be grateful for the serious-minded purpose and industry it displayed, and the objective approach it demonstrated in dealing with this difficult program.
As I have already noted, the program recommended by the committee, and now being enacted by the government, is substantially the same as that first proposed to the provinces in 1945.
When the measure is taken by later generations of recent progress in Canada, it will be seen even more clearly than now that this

generation of Canadians has developed an enlarged concept of social justice and a recognition of the fact that in our parliamentary democratic society the highest responsibility of government is to promote the well-being of its people.
The history of this quarter-century from 1926 to 1951, beginning with the abortive effort to pass our first old age pensions act and coming to fruition in this year's vast and comprehensive old age security program, is the story of our awakening as a nation to a new understanding of what can be done, through government, for our older citizens and their security.
This concern for our senior citizens is the touchstone to the true quality of our way of life. It is one of the proofs of our claim to a civilization, inspired by the immutable principles on which our society has been founded. It is one of the best signs of the strength of the democracy we cherish.
What we are doing today to provide assistance for Canadian men and women at 65, and what we will do before this year is out to complete our pattern for old age security, will bring Canada in this field into the forefront of the nations of the world. Canada's old age security program is a symbol of our determination to work for the well-being of all our citizens. This humanitarian action, like every measure for social progress, helps to counter communism and all other alien and heartless systems in which the individual, young or old, is the last and not the first concern of government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES- PAYMENTS AT AGE 65
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt the house will give unanimous support to the motion for second reading of this bill.
It may be one of the curious anomalies of debate in this house that the importance of a measure is not always indicated by the length of time spent in discussing it. It seems to me this bill is so clear and simple and limited in its terms that it need not give rise to a lengthy debate. For my part I think I can put my views on the principle of the bill into a relatively brief compass.
The bill, as compared with the statements which preceded it and the limited information given the house by the minister two days ago at the resolution stage, contains no particular surprises. When one expresses gratification that this bill has been introduced and has reached the present stage, one should not be taken as indicating complete satisfaction with the bill, or as entertaining the view that this is the answer to all hopes and the last word in legislation of this kind. The house will recognize at once the importance of the measure. The house will see in its
Old Age Assistance Act adoption today the culmination, in part, of the efforts of many people in this country and many members of this house, and the devoted efforts of all parties here to bring about a more comprehensive and adequate measure of security for those of our citizens who have reached advanced years and reduced earning power.
I think we would not do justice to the measure, however, if we did not endeavour to view it in true perspective, having regard especially to the emphasis placed by the minister in his remarks today on the part played by the special committee of both houses on social security which sat during the session of 1950, and on whose recommendations the government obviously has drawn so largely in preparing this bill.
This, of course, is an enabling bill. It could not be otherwise, having regard to the constitutional limitations imposed upon the power of parliament. That has some disadvantages, of course, from the point of view of parliament. It means that far more power is given to the government in the matter of negotiating agreements with the provinces than many of us like to see given. We like to see more of the provisions of important legislation of this, kind written into the terms of the bill rather than left to be determined by cabinet decision. In the second place, it must be a participating scheme on the part of the dominion and the provinces, with administration vested in the provinces. That is inescapable unless parliament were to adopt a scheme of universal pensions in this age group 65 to 69 as well as in the higher age group of 70 and over; and, of course, that has not been done.
The second disadvantage that flows from the fact that in its nature this is enabling legislation is that in effect the dominion is imposing certain terms which are set out in the bill. They are not loose and easy terms. In many respects they are rather stiff. It is true that this morning, at an opportune time, the minister announced a relaxation in the rigour of some of those terms, which I think the house will welcome. Nevertheless it means that in the type of scheme to which the bill commits the country the dominion does lay down certain terms which the provinces must meet if they are to receive a fifty per cent contribution from the dominion toward the cost of assistance for the age group 65 to 69.
I am afraid we are going to bring about a continuation of that not too happy situation where, when complaints do arise out of the administration of the act, and recipients of the assistance come up against some of the harder features of the terms laid down, we shall hear from the government the familiar
4554	HOUSE OF
Old Age Assistance Act excuse: That is a matter for the provinces; the provinces administer the scheme and therefore the responsibility must rest upon them. It seems to me that argument has never been fair to the provinces, having regard to the fact the dominion does lay down the basic terms upon which assistance may be obtained by the provinces toward provision made for pensions.
Let us be perfectly frank in dealing with this subject, and in facing, as we are bound to face, the problems that will arise in the future out of the administration of this scheme under the provinces. Let us be prepared to acknowledge, when these difficulties do arise, that they arise because the dominion lays down certain terms with which the provinces must comply, and the responsibility for the resultant condition is not fairly to be laid at the door of the provinces. I say that by way of seeking clarification of the situation and a frank and honest treatment of the kind of problem that is likely to arise in that respect from the type of measure that is under discussion.
There are several other provisions of this bill that merit comment in this debate. When commenting on these I naturally draw attention to those which fall short of meeting the hopes that one might have entertained for a measure of this kind. I draw attention also to these problems so that they can be viewed in their proper perspective. We do not wish the importance of this measure, or the benefits that are likely to flow from it, desirable as they are, to be exaggerated or misunderstood.
In the first place, the minister has drawn attention to the fact that this is a measure to give assistance. I think there is much to be said for the selection of the word "assistance", as being more properly descriptive of the type of benefits held out in this bill for the age group 65 to 69, than the word "pension". It is a much more appropriate word, and I am glad to see it in use.
I was happy to hear the minister put some emphasis upon it this morning.
I believe that any tendency to exaggerate the importance of the measure will be modified when we have regard to the amounts involved. We have heard a figure of $410 million used. Let us bear in mind that only a very small fraction of that is required for the scheme set forth in this bill concerning assistance for those in the 65 to 69 group. The great bulk of the expenditure that is to be provided this year by parliament for the assistance of persons of senior age goes, of course, to provide the universal pension for those 70 years of age


and over. By comparison with the amount involved under that measure, the amount at stake in this measure is relatively small. The bill contemplates the joint expenditure by the dominion and the provinces of $64 million per year, of which the dominion will contribute $32 million per year. The number who are likely to receive benefits under the bill, as the minister has indicated and as the committee estimated last year, is approximately 145,000. Those estimates, of course, cannot be expected to be too exact.
It will be interesting to see, in the light of experience during the first year or two of the life of this scheme, how many of the 145,000 persons will receive the full assistance contemplated by the bill, and how many will receive only a portion of it. Let us bear in mind that as long as this type of assistance follows the test that we are accustomed to call the means test, then obviously many persons are going to derive only partial benefits from the assistance scheme.
One interesting feature which I believe calls for comment, Mr. Speaker, is the monthly amount. The maximum established under this bill is $40, and that follows the recommendation of the committee. I think the members of the committee were conscious of the fact that $40 in 1950,- when they made their recommendation, was worth only about sixty cents per dollar in terms of pre-war purchasing power. Of course, that purchasing power has undergone a further shrinkage in the year that has elapsed since the committee tendered its report to parliament. Nevertheless, the problem of financing and the problem of inaugurating a new type of scheme with a new type of benefit called for a measure of caution on the part of the committee, and that has been carried forward into the present measure.
One of the leading features of this measure is the retention of the means test. I believe the minister has indicated some desire to skate away from that term, which has acquired, over the period of the last generation, a rather ugly meaning in the minds of many people. We more frequently hear from the minister the term "eligibility test".. The term may be a more polite expression, but I am afraid, sir, we have here the same' old means test in all its essentials. In dealing, with this point the minister has, in justification of this feature of the measure, put, forward two arguments. In the first place,, he has relied upon the recommendation of the committee, and, in the second place, he has drawn attention, quite properly, to the very great cost that would be involved.

When I spoke on the resolution stage of this measure two days ago, I reviewed as best I could the problem the committee faced in connection with the means test. It caused the special committee a great deal of difficulty. If the diligent chairman of that committee (Mr. Lesage) speaks on this measure, I am sure he will fully bear me out in that regard. The means test was condemned by almost every organization which sent representatives to the committee, and by almost every person experienced in the operation of the Old Age Pensions Act who testified. Our attention was drawn to the fact that the test inevitably penalizes the thrifty and creates unwarrantable intrusions on the part of state officials into the private affairs of the individual. Admittedly the means test did give rise to a certain undeniable degree of imposition on the authorities, because this means test, as we were freely told, had been improperly defeated by a good many applicants by reason of nondisclosure.
At best it is a difficult test to enforce, and the committee, therefore, Mr. Speaker, without a dissenting voice, recommended to the house that the means test ought to be abolished as to the age group 70 years of age and over.
There may at once appear to be a fundamental contradiction in the recommendations of the committee in proposing, on the one hand, that the means test should be abolished as to the age group 70 years and over, and1, on the other hand, that an eligibility test be retained for those in the age group 65 to 69. Well, sir, there is undeniably a measure of contradiction there. I think the house might as well be candid, and recognize the fact that the means test as applied to the age group 65 to 69 can hardly be expected to operate much more satisfactorily as to this group than it has been working with respect to the group 70 years of age and over. The bill maintains the essential elements of the same scheme, with all its objectionable features, in the new measures providing assistance to those 65 to 69. You are going to impose a relative penalty upon thrift; you are going to have the same kind of intrusion into the affairs of individuals; you are going to have the same difficulty of enforcement; you are going to have the same army of inspectors going about inquiring into the affairs of people.
Those of us on that committee who gave our consent to the report because it contained so much of value that everyone must recognize-at the same time regretting very much that force of circumstances, and particularly the cost, obliged the committee as to
Old Age Assistance Act the group 65 to 69 to confine itself to a scheme of continuing the eligibility test- will feel free, Mr. Speaker, to say here today that if we indulge in prophecy we shall not be surprised if, as the years advance and this new scheme for assistance to the group 65 to 69 begins to operate under the tests prescribed in this measure, we have the same difficulties, the same injustices in many cases as have existed hitherto. This, therefore, cannot be regarded as a final solution of this problem.
It is a compromise measure of the kind we accept so often in the house on the basis that it will greatly improve the present situation, will remove some of the present stresses on the social and economic fabric in the case of necessitous persons in this particular group. But it is not a satisfactory solution of the problem. I think on that point there will not be any great difference of opinion among those who sat on the committee. I think we all viewed with a measure of reluctance a recommendation that carried with it the same deficiencies that we had already condemned in the same test as to the group 70 years of age and over.
Now, sir, the other factor that the minister mentioned was the question of cost. Undoubtedly the provision of universal pensions for this group 65 to 69 would have involved an enormous cost. Bear in mind that the figures that the minister has given this morning, and the type of argument that he has used-and it runs through the report of the committee and the summary of the evidence which the report contains-picture the alternative as a universal pension at age 65. As time goes on and more experience is gained and more information collated in the light of administration of this new measure, it may be-and some of us will continue to be hopeful of this-that we shall devise within the age group 65 to 69, without going the full way to the universal pension which would be so enormously costly, some other method which will be better than the means test, and will be related to a system of financing which will be fair to all concerned.
There is a great problem. The committee did not have the final answer to it, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, that we shall look upon the views of the committee in this regard and on the present measure as of a somewhat tentative nature; that we shall examine closely, especially in the next two or three years, the operations of the new scheme as to the age group 65 to 69 and gather information; for there is much information to be gathered. The committee did one of its most useful
4556	HOUSE OF
Old Age Assistance Act pieces of work in gathering up under one cover a mass of information that had not been gathered together and centralized in that form before. There will be, I feel sure, a gold mine of information to be gathered in these next several years as the new scheme comes into operation and is administered.
The next feature of the measure that I should like to comment upon arises out of the means test, or at least is related to it. I refer to the permission to earn outside income, what the minister has, I think in somewhat exaggerated terms, referred to as encouragement that the bill gives to the earning of supplemental income on the part of this group. Sir, much has been made of the fact that the present supplemental income allowed under the Old Age Pensions Act, namely $120 a year, or $10 a month, is enlarged by this measure, as to the group 65 to 69, to $240 a year, or $20 a month. But the dollar has been stretched further in the past twelve months since the recommendation was made, and when the minister suggests that this represents more generous treatment than that accorded to such people anywhere else in the wide world, I think he is indulging in hyperbolical flights of fancy. Looking, Mr. Speaker, at the commendable purpose that the minister himself admitted, which justified earning of income on the part of this group, surely to confine that income to $20 a month in the case of an individual-and if you please, a total of $20 a month in the case of a married couple, both of whom are under old age pension, provided that neither of them is blind-is, it seems to me, not having very much regard to a realistic approach to methods by which we may attain the purpose that the minister has endorsed.
The minister says we want to encourage people in this age group to work. We do. But if earnings of a married couple are going to be confined to $20 a month, I do not think there is much inducement left for those people to go out and work. I do not see much encouragement there; 1 do not see much recognition there of some of the incontestable facts laid before the committee by those who came before it with their testimony.
We had statements from leaders in industry that the tendency in industry today is not toward the retirement of people at 65. The value of the services of persons in the age group 65-69, was emphasized by leaders in industry, because in that group there is a stability and reliability among those physically able to continue in employment which industry is today increasingly recognizing.


The type of scheme which compels retirement from industrial employment of employees at the age of 65, we were given to understand, is not so likely to be encouraged in future, because of the usefulness in industry of citizens of that group.
If those views commended themselves to the committee a year ago, surely, Mr. Speaker, they are even more entitled today to recognition because of the limitations on our labour force and the tremendous demands that are to be put upon that labour force to meet the growing needs of our defence program. Therefore one must express regret and disappointment that the amount of supplemental income allowed is not adequate realistically to meet or to attain the objectives which are admitted as worthy of general support.
What about persons who, by their thrift, have made provision at this age for their later years? What about the type of industrial pension which takes effect at this age? It means that the person in industry who ha? submitted to deductions from his pay envelopes over the years to provide his contributory portion toward his industrial retirement pension will have deducted from his claim to benefits under this act the full amount of his industrial pension. Obviously that is a weakness in the bill, and it points to the inadequacy of this provision for the earning of supplemental income.
One other matter that has been touched upon, and does relate to the means test, is recovery from the estates of recipients. I am happy indeed that the minister has seen fit, even at this eleventh hour, to withdraw the requirement that the provinces, when entering into agreements with the dominion, should be compelled to recover from the estates of recipients and share the recovery equally with the dominion. I am glad that has been withdrawn. But bear in mind that what has been withdrawn is the compulsory feature. The minister made it clear this morning that if any province chooses to recover from the estates of recipients, then the dominion will share equally in the proceeds. I hope no encouragement will be offered to any province to follow a scheme of that kind; because the committee had an abundance of evidence to show that the recoveries from estates of recipients of old age pensions were negligible. The deputy minister was probably the leading witness on the point, and the expression he used, in reply to a question was, as I recall it, "virtually negligible".
We will wish to know why those in receipt of war veterans allowances under this bill

are singled out for special mention; but that is a matter for the committee stage.
Finally, the whole question of financing a scheme of this kind should have received, in my view, much more ample treatment than it received in the scant reference to it by the minister this morning. We have been kept in the dark until this morning as to the method by which the cost of this scheme is to be met.
When the Prime Minister made his announcement on the subject on June 4, he said, as reported at page 3665 of Hansard:
Moreover, as hon. members know, the universal pensions are to have right from the start a contributory basis.
Now, the Prime Minister did not make any reference at that time to the method by which the cost of the old age assistance for the group 65 to 69 is to be met-not a word on the subject. If parliament is to see this problem whole, as it should; if this is one whole problem of old age security, not two problems divided into watertight compartments at the age of seventy, then what we should have before the house now is a comprehensive outline and detail of the method by which the whole cost of both branches of the scheme is to be financed.
We have not been given that. We are told to wait until next fall before we know anything about the method by which the cost of the universal pension at the age of 70 is to be met. We are told simply that it is to be a "contributory" pension. Well, that word could cover a multitude of different methods of meeting the cost. But we are left completely in the dark at this stage as to what the method will be. We have waited until this morning to know how the cost of the benefits for the group 65 to 69 is to be met. Following the minister in his brief reference to this subject this morning as closely as one could, one infers that the cost is simply to be met out of the consolidated revenue fund; there is no special provision as to the source of the funds to meet this scheme.

And, Mr. Speaker, I attach such importance to this whole question of old age security and to the importance of seeing the problem whole, and the importance therefore of seeing how from the beginning we are to
Old Age Assistance Act provide the cost for the whole scheme, that I must express my strong regret that our information on this vital aspect of the problem is so very meagre today.
When people go to purchase even those things they want most, they do not do it on the basis of being told: Well, come back in three or four months and we will tell you how it is to be paid for. People usually like to know how they are going to pay for the things they buy before they make the purchase. I cannot see why in this respect the people of Canada should be placed in any different position from the average man or housewife who goes to the store to make a purchase. He or she wants to know what the cost is. We have been given an indication as to the cost; and he or she wants to know at the same time how that price is to be paid. We are not told that. I think the house wants to know more about that subject and should have been given more information.
That brings me back to the point I started to make when speaking on Thursday, that we should have approached this problem with both measures for treatment of the problem before us. I have reviewed what seemed to me to be many of the important features of this bill, and have drawn attention to them in the hope that there will be a realistic appreciation, not only of those important points but also of the limitations of the bill. I urge that the house do not content itself with the enactment of these measures today and then sit back and think that its task is completed. I urge the house to regard the step that it is taking today, important and far-reaching as it is, as only a tentative step. It should be a recognition of our desire, in the light of the experience we will quickly gather through the administration of this scheme, to keep closely in touch with the problem, studying it from month to month and seeking ever to eliminate the difficulties and problems that will inevitably arise in the administration of it.

In speaking to the second reading of this bill I wish to say, first of all, that I regard it as a most welcome piece of legislation. Indeed this is an historic occasion. We are providing for the first time in Canadian history for the payment of old age pensons, at least to some Canadians below the age of 70 years. I shall have something to say as to the progress yet to be made, and I shall endeavour to indicate some of the points that I feel must be pursued. In doing so I hope that I shall not be accused of detracting in any way from the importance and the significance of the measure now before us. Indeed,

Old Age Assistance Act a little later in my remarks I intend to draw attention to some of the specific features of the bill now before us which I regard as exceptionally good.
However, like the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Fleming), I feel that this is not the time for members of parliament to sit back and feel satisfied that the job is done. As I have indicated already, we are taking an important step; we are inaugurating pensions for some of our fellow citizens between the ages of 65 and 69 years. But this is only the opening chapter and not the end of the story. I urge most strongly upon all hon. members that they continue to give thought to this important problem. Eight now while we are taking this important step is indeed the time to think of the other steps that have yet to be taken before we shall have completely rounded out an adequate program of old age security as part of an adequate program of over-all social security.
I should like for just a minute to refer to something we were discussing two or three days ago under another item. I would emphasize the fact that once we have taken the important steps in the field of old age security that we are taking this year, the gap with respect to health insurance will be all the more apparent. I feel that we must give close and serious attention to that problem. References are being made to the good work that was done by last year's committee on old age security, and I was glad to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) state the other night that the government is giving consideration to the setting up of a similar committee in 1952 to go into the whole question of health insurance. That is an important part of any over-all social security program. Indeed we owe it, not only to all Canadians but to our elder citizens about whom we are thinking today, to see to it that a program of health insurance is included in our social security arrangements.
With regard to the work yet to be done in the field of old age pensions, and in particular with regard to those in the age group from 65 to 69, I submit, as I have indicated already, that there are two improvements that we shall have to make. We shall have to start agitating for those improvements just as soon as this present job is done. On the one hand, we shall have to do something about the amount of the pension, and on the other hand, we shall have to abolish the means test from the pension for those from 65 to 69.
A $40 pension as compared with the $20 which was the old age pension as recently as 1942 and the early part of 1943 sounds like


progress. As the Minister of National Health and Welfare pointed out this morning, that means that in less than a decade we have actually doubled the amount of the old age pension in terms of dollars. But in view of the continuing rise in the cost of living we must face the fact that that $40 today is not worth what it was back in the days when the old age pension legislation first came into being. As I pointed out the other day, in terms of the 1935-39 purchasing power of the dollar, $40 today is worth only $21.97. In other words, we are starting off the group from 65 to 69 years at just about the same point as that at which we started those of 70 years and over back in 1927.
I feel I should repeat the point I made the other day, to the effect that the increase in the cost of living from last June to the present time has decreased the value of $40, even in terms of its purchasing power last June, to a figure of a little over $36. In other words, if we were fully to implement the recommendations of last year's committee for a pension of $40 a month for those between the ages of 65 and 69 years in terms of the purchasing power of $40 when that recommendation was made, the amount proposed by the minister in the bill today should be not less than $44. I contend that in view of continuing increases in the cost of living, and in view of our increased productivity across the years, the day has come when we shall have to think in terms of old age retirement pensions at a figure of at least $60 a month for all our senior citizens.
I expect that some hon. members will suggest that that is a large figure; that the cost will be great. It may be asked whether I have given any thought to that aspect of the matter. First of all, may I say that I have in my hand Hansard for February 28, 1938, the daily edition. This well-worn booklet is over thirteen years old. On that day Mr. A. A. Heaps, who was then the member for Winnipeg North, seconded by the then and present member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), moved a resolution with respect to old age pensions. There have been a good many resolutions and amendments respecting old age pensions moved from this corner of the house across the years, relating from time to time to different aspects of the old age pension problem. On that occasion, and that is one reason why I produce this copy of Hansard, the particular point covered by the motion moved by Mr. Heaps and seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East was that the eligible age for old age pensions should be lowered. The motion dealt with that point only. It was a very interesting debate, in which some who are still members of the

house took part, and in which a part was taken by some who are no longer here. The minister involved was the then minister of finance, Mr. Dunning. Mr. Dunning pointed out at page 892 of the copy of Hansard I have in my hand that the cost of old age pensions to the federal government in the year 1938 had already risen to the staggering figure of $30 million. He suggested that one had to approach the motion debated on that day with extreme caution, because if it were carried, if indeed the age limit were brought down to 65 and a pension of $20 a month paid at that time, it would have increased the federal government's expenditure on old age pensions to the impossible sum of $48 million a year.
I have no doubt that in those days members who talked in terms of such figures thought they were extremely large, but today even under the present act the federal government is spending more than $100 million a year on old age pensions, and the total commitments involved in the program of old age legislation for this year will be something over $350 million a year. In other words, the times do move on, and figures that seem large on one occasion become quite small in later years. Incidentally Mr. Dunning's final words, in speaking with caution, if I may put it that way, on Mr. Heaps' motion were:
I believe we would be hindering rather than helping the ultimate solution by plunging in the direction the hon. member for Winnipeg North desires us to plunge.
That was the attitude of the Liberal minister of finance in 1938, that to propose to lower the old age pension age to 65 was a plunge that could not be taken. I am glad that we now have in the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) a man who is prepared to take that plunge and to bring in a bill lowering the age to 65.

If these changes were made,
I will indicate what the result would be. We would find that the total number of Canadians 65 years of age and over would amount to about seven per cent of the total population of the country. If we paid all of them a pension of $60 a month, or $720 a year, we would be diverting to them something in the order of 3j per cent of our gross national product, or 3J per cent of our current production. I suggest that is the basis upon which we should view this matter. I suggest it is not unfair to ask that seven per cent of our population, our older people who have contributed to the building up of the country, who have produced great wealth throughout their working years, should be entitled to 3J per cent of the wealth that the country is able to produce, and able to do so very largely because of the contribution that they have made throughout the years.
In this connection I noted on Thursday that the Minister of National Health and Welfare quite properly said that attention was being paid to the recommendations of last year's committee not only within Canada but in other countries. He referred in particular to the fact that in the United States some real note was being taken of the studies and conclusions that our committee reached. I have in my hand a copy of a document entitled Business Conditions, published by the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago. This issue is in fact devoted wholly to the question of old age pensions. There are a number of interesting articles in it, and although there is no direct reference by name to Canada or to our old age security committee, it is pretty obvious to those of us who were members of the committee that the people who wrote this document had studied the work done by our committee. I find on page 10 an article entitled "Economics of Old Age Pensions", containing two or three interesting comments, one or two of which I should like to read. The first is:
Regardless of whether the dollar cost of pensions is measured in terms of the annual payment liability, the expense of funding past and current service credits, or the amount necessary to provide an individual annuity at retirement, the real cost of providing pensions in terms of goods and services will be borne at the time the pensions are paid.
That is the basic principle with respect to old age security that we in this corner of the house have been enunciating during the
4560	HOUSE OF
Old Age Assistance Act years that our movement has been represented here. The real cost of providing pensions in terms of goods and services will be borne at the time that the pensions are paid. What I like most of all about the over-all program that is being introduced at this time is that it is based on the pay as we go principle, that it is based on a recognition of the fact that old age pensions and other forms of security are paid not out of some fund that is set apart somewhere, but out of the current production of a country such as ours.
On that basis I suggest that one should look again at the percentages I gave a moment ago. I repeat that it is not unfair to suggest that seven per cent of our population, our older people who have taken their turn at the work of the nation, should enjoy in their retirement some 3 j per cent of the wealth that the country is producing. This same article, having emphasized the point that the real cost of providing pensions is borne at the time the pensions are paid, goes on to state the truth that if you pay larger pensions they have to come out of the current production and therefore that has an effect on the standard of living of the entire country. The article then goes on to say:
For this reason, it is important that as many older people as possible be retained in productive jobs past the age of 65, provided they do not displace younger and more efficient workers. It is estimated that there are about three million persons 65 years and older in the labour force at the present time-
The reference is to the United States.
-and that their contribution to output during 1949 amounted to about $11 billion. To the extent that these older people can be kept employed, the real costs of old age security will be lessened, and the general standard of living will be higher.
The word "real" in that quotation is italicized. I submit that if that basic principle is to be accepted-and I believe it is sound- we have to go a great deal further in the direction of encouraging people from 65 to 69 to earn supplementary income than is provided for in even the relaxed form of means test in the bill now before us. In fact I have already made it clear that I think we have to go the whole way and remove the means test at 65. I want to repeat that this is not to be interpreted as detracting one iota from my statement of how welcome this measure is and how pleased I am that we are getting started with a pension payable at 65; but I submit I am demonstrating this morning that when some of us ask for the complete removal of the means test at 65 we are not just asking for something out of thin air, but are stating fundamental economic principles that are extremely important to the kind of economy in which we are living today.


So I leave that phase of it for the moment. I have tried, as I say, to chart the future course we must follow. It is good that we are taking this step, but we still have a long way to go. In the meantime, with regard to old age pensions themselves, two things yet must be done. We must get the amount of the pension increased, and I submit that it should now be $60 a month; and we should get the means test off at age 65.
In connection with that figure of $60 a month, I remind the house that in the early part of 1949 there was tabled in this house from this group a petition containing more than a quarter of a million signatures, asking for a pension of $50 a month at 65 without a means test. Incidentally the report of the clerk of petitions was that that petition was in order. At the time it was regarded by some hon. members as asking a little too much. In the interval, however, the rise in the cost of living has made it clear that there was one thing wrong with that petition; the amount asked for should have been higher. And it is clearer than ever to me, particularly because of the studies we undertook in last year's committee, that the means test should come off at 65.
In his remarks this morning the minister said the view of the committee was that the principle of universality should not be applied to the group 65 to 69. I submit that is not quite what the committee said. These were its words:
There is an advantage in universality when the large majority of the age group concerned is retired. That advantage does not obtain to the same extent when the majority of the age group concerned is still active and self-supporting.
That is quite a different thing from saying the committee took the view that the principle of universality should not be applied in this group. I have looked through the act, and that is the story for every category; whatever the maximum ceiling was before, it has been increased by $10 a month. I have already indicated, and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has done so as well, that despite the minister's statement that in his view the bill fully implements the recommendations of the committee, I do not believe that allowing a total of $20 a month of other income really carries out the recommendation that we should recognize to a greater extent than at present the desirability of encouraging recipients to earn supplemental income, as was recommended by the committee. I refer again to my quotations from the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago. I suggest that to tell people they can earn other income of $20 a month without suffering a reduction in their pension really is not very much encouragement for them to go out and work and earn other income, to say nothing of the loss to our total economy from the lack of such encouragement.

Old Age Assistance Act should have been raised to a higher amount than is proposed in the bill. In fact, I had hoped that some regard might be paid to the income tax exemption levels. Surely those figures indicate the minimum amounts upon which people can be expected to live. So far as the old age pensioners in this bracket are concerned, they are being asked to live on much lower maximum amounts.
Apart from that, Mr. Speaker, there is one matter to which I feel I must register strong objection. The present Old Age Pensions Act has been on the statute book for more than twenty-four years. We have had that many years' experience in this field. During the whole of those twenty-four years there have been only two years, namely from 1949 to the present time, when the allowable income was the same for a married couple as it was for a single person. I regret that that idea is being carried forward in this bill. This bill provides that $20 per month is to be the other income allowed to a single person, and the same amount is to be allowed a married couple.
In the original act which became effective in 1927, the allowable income was $125 per year for a single person and $250 for a married couple. In other words, it was approximately $10 per month for a single person and $20 per month for a married couple. It stayed that way until 1943. In that year, by virtue of an accident, the amount of other income was reduced to $65 per year for a single person and $130 per year for a married couple. The effect of that accident was such that there were many complaints about it. It was not many months until Mr. Ilsley, who was then the minister of finance, corrected the situation by order in council, and restored the amount of other income to the figures provided in the original act.
The act stayed that way until 1947, when the pension was increased to $30 per month for a single person and $60 per month for married couples, and the ceilings on total income were raised to $600 per year for single persons and $1,080 for married couples. This meant that a single person was allowed $20 per month of other income, while married couples were allowed $30 per month. I respect the thinking behind that decision. I believe it was sound that a married couple should have more than a single person, and I think there was something to be said for the married couple's greater amount being not twice as much but in some such proportion as was worked out. I point out that the decision made in 1947 was deliberate. It was a decision of the people who drafted the act brought in at that time, and it was a decision consciously made.


But in 1949, when the amount of pension was increased to $40, by a sheer accident, indeed by virtue of the fact that no change was made in the ceilings on total income, we were left with the situation that a single person was allowed only $10 per month other income and a married couple were allowed the same figure. The ceilings of $600 per year and $1,080 per year were left, and we got that accidental result of the same amount for a single person as for a married couple. I recognize the plausibility in what the government is now doing. They are applying the $10 per month or $120 per year increase across the board. What they are doing though, Mr. Speaker, is adding the same amount across the board to a basis which is already wrong, a basis which was not arrived at by any conscious thought on the part of the people who drafted the legislation, but which was arrived at accidentally. I submit it is most unfortunate that this accident of 1949 is being carried forward at this time when we are setting up this new piece of legislation. I repeat that we have had old age pension experience in this country for twenty-four years, and for twenty-two out of the twenty-four years a greater amount of other income was allowed to married couples than to a single person. As this error for only two years out of twenty-four was brought about by accident, I submit most strongly there is no justification for carrying forward that wrong.
There are other matters that I should like to have spoken about, but I shall not carry the debate past one o'clock. I can deal with the other matters I want to speak about when we get into committee. As the minister will be aware from the way I have just spoken, when we reach the section dealing with other income I shall strongly urge him to consider an amendment. It is extremely unfortunate at this time to carry forward that mistake by making the other income allowed a married couple the same as that allowed a single person and so small an amount at that. I hope a change can be made in that at this time.
I conclude by saying, as I said at the beginning, that I welcome this legislation. I am glad to be here when we are starting old age pensions at the age of 65, but we have still a long way to go to achieve complete old age security, including justice and fair play to our elder citizens. I, for one, will carry on the fight for improvement in the position of our older people.

In addition to what I have already said, the province of Alberta at present extends medical, dental, optical and hospital services to pensioners who qualify, over 70 years of age, at a cost of $3.50 per month each. What about that program? Where will the province find the money, let us say, to extend those same services to pensioners from 65 to 69, and thus escape the charge of discrimination? That is a problem they have to face-and it is a real one.
Moreover, let us not forget that there is no distinction made in this bill between white people and our Indian brethren. They are all placed on a level. The fact that the Indian population is brought into the assistance scheme places another burden on the provinces. So I am simply saying this, that somebody has to recognize the burden that the provinces are to be asked to carry. Instead of standing up here and whining about the whole thing being inadequate, let us just take a look at it from the provincial point of view. Let us remember that when the provinces feel that they are ready to ask for more generous allowances for these people, they will likely come along and ask; and at that time we should support them to the fullest of our ability.
Another observation I should make about the bill is that it is doubtless a monument to several things. In the first place I think it is a monument-and I say this first because it comes to my mind first, not because I believe it is the one that requires priority-it is a monument to the persistence of those people in the house, no matter on what side they
[Mr. Ferried

may have sat, who, over the years, have demanded a better deal for our aged citizens.
I am satisfied that the government, including the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will admit that the members of the opposition in all parties-a good many of them at least-have been as tenacious as the proverbial pup that got hold of a root. And it has been pulling on it ever since. I say that the bill is a monument to their tenacity and determination of purpose. At the same time we will have to say that it stands as a monument to the recognition by the government of the determination of the people of Canada to get better conditions for the aged people. So we give them credit for recognizing that fact and yielding to pressure.
For us to stand here and to debate where credit should go would be foolish. I do not think it should matter to us who gets the credit as long as the aged people get the cash. That is the position I take.
As to the adequacy of the assistance, as it is called in the bill: I think that neither the amount of the assistance nor the amount of the supplementary earnings allowable under the bill will be considered sufficient by any thinking person to provide a good standard of living for these aged people. I certainly do not think it is adequate in either case. The purchasing value of the maximum income allowed under the bill is, under present circumstances, pitifully small. We wish it could be greater; but when one considers along with that the burden of taxation that is now borne by the Canadian people, and what would have to be borne if the assistance were to be granted at a higher level, one wonders with a great deal of sobriety just how much further we can go with this and other kinds of social security measures so long as the government has to depend entirely upon taxation to get money.
Some new approach will simply have to be found if we are ever to have in Canada an adequate old age or, for that matter, any other kind of security program. I speak of another approach. I know something about another approach; but I only mention it briefly by way of indicating that there is some way by which such things can be done.
I happen to be a member of a group of people who have succeeded in establishing a social assistance program based upon actual need, and who did succeed during the hungry thirties in taking practically every single one of its members off government assistance an'fi relief. It did that without taxing anybody a five cent piece. Ways were found by that

group of people of providing those needs without drawing from or diminishing in any way the national commercial stockpile. A fine type of co-operative effort and enterprise added a supplementary stockpile, if you wish to call it that, to the nation's commercial stockpile. And it was and at present is out of this supplement, or increased production, that material assistance is drawn by the disabled and the unfortunate. No financial currency is involved.
I am suggesting simply that there is a way of doing it without taxing the daylights out of the people. If it is possible in the instance I have suggested, in broad outline, to find a way of inducing people to put forth an effort to build a stockpile of goods and services which can be distributed among the unemployed, the disabled and the unemployable, I suggest that it can be done on a national scale, if we bend our efforts in that direction.
I say that until such time as we can induce the all-out productive effort that will provide supplementary stockpiles that are not involved in financial and commercial intricacies, I am satisfied that we are not going to be able to go too fast in the expansion of social security programs of any kind.
There is a natural resistance on the part of people everywhere to excessive taxation, and we must recognize that fact. We have to pay some attention to the people who, in the long run, pay the taxes. We have to find means of providing an adequate standard of living for our people-our aged, our unemployables and, particularly, our disabled -that does not involve the present intricacies of taxation or borrowing.
I do not want to prolong the discussion. I shall wish to make some comments on certain sections as they come along, but I want to conclude by saying that we in the Social Credit group look forward to the time when old age pensions and old age assistance of the kind that we are providing in this bill will become one of the mechanisms by which additions to the money supply of Canada will be made as and when those additions are required, without adding interest or tax burdens upon the people. That sort of mechanism will simply have to be used if we are ever to preserve any measure of personal independence among the Canadian people and get rid of the injustices and oppressions that our present financial policy visits upon the people.
Until we reach that happy stage in our progress toward full social security for all, with a maximum of personal freedom, it seems to me that no adequate pension can ever be paid. So let us work forward to the
Old Age Assistance Act day when some new technique such as the one I have discussed will be made possible of application in this dominion, and then we will not have to worry too much about means tests or anything of the sort we have in this bill. We support the principle of this bill.
