On behalf of the committee I should like to pay tribute to the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Finance, the Department of Labour and the Department of Justice, who helped us so much in our work and who spared nothing in order to be at our disposal at all times. In particular, the staff of the research branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare showed an interest and devotion which went far beyond what their duty required of them.
I know it is always dangerous to single out any one in particular, but I believe in the present case no one will be offended if I personally, and in the name of the members of the committee, pay a special tribute to a man who for months worked for the committee day and night. His talent, his knowledge, his clear mind, his affable manner did more to bring about a happy solution of the problems we were discussing than anything else. I think this man deserves the gratitude of parliament and indeed of the Canadian people. I refer to the deputy minister of welfare, Dr. Davidson.
I think I can say in the name of the members of the committee that we are grateful to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), and to the government for having accepted the conclusions of the committee as the basis for the proposed legislation on old age security. We appreciate

Old Age Assistance Act also that the provinces responded to the appeal contained in the last words of the report, and I quote:
The committee trusts that the views herein set forth will appeal to the provincial governments as worthy of favourable consideration.
The provincial governments have answered that appeal and with the magnificent cooperation of the eleven governments of this country it is now possible to have before us legislation implementing the conclusions of the committee.
I listened with great interest on Thursday and again this morning to the debate that took place on the principle of the bill, or as a matter of fact on the whole question of old age security. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), the committee in its deliberations was confronted with three main aspects of an old age security program. The first was the means test; the second was the question of age; and the third was the amount of the benefit or pension. One question which was asked of practically all the witnesses was which one of the following courses they would give priority to: abolishing the means test, lowering the age, or increasing the amount of pension. The practically unanimous answer was that first priority should be given to doing away with the means test for people 70 years of age and over; that second priority should be given to lowering the age to 65 years; and that third priority should be given to considering an increase in the amount of the pension. The conclusions of the committee were reached accordingly.
Let us not forget that the program which the government has accepted follows the conclusions of the committee in its main lines. As the minister said this morning, there is only one slight difference in connection with residence and this was for obvious reasons which will be explained by the minister. The conclusions of the committee were based on briefs presented by organizations and testimony given by representatives of organizations representing practically all classes in Canada. Let us not forget that.
The program which the government is ready to implement will be in accord with our conclusions. The means test is to be done away with as far as people of 70 years and over are concerned. The age has been reduced to 65 following an understanding reached with the provinces at the end of May. It has been said, and I expected that it would be, by the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that the eligibility test was too much like the means test, and that the restrictions on other income were not lifted

sufficiently. May I borrow the words of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and say that we are dealing with a matter in connection with which we must have the concurrence of the provinces.
During the meetings of the federal-provincial conference, in which I had the honour to participate, most of the provinces were reluctant to see the income ceiling increased from the figures that we now have for people 70 and over. Only one or two provinces asked for an increase in the income ceiling. Therefore the government felt that the increase should be a reasonable one but that at the same time the provinces should be free to accept it or to accept any amount below the maximum ceiling. Therefore the provinces which have asked for an increased ceiling may use it if they want to and the ones which object to it will do whatever they like.
We have to respect the autonomy of the provinces. Even if I am a Liberal from Quebec, no one will be surprised if I say that, and this is one instance in which we have to work hand in hand with the provinces. The provinces expressed their fear of the financial and economic impact of too great a liberalization of the eligibility test for people between 65 and 69. This test may have different effects as applied to people between 65 and 69 from what it has had when applied to those 70 and over. It is not the same age group. The economic and financial effects may very well be different, and the provinces expressed the hope that the federal government would wait for a while before going too far with any increase of the income ceiling. They have expressed the hope that they might be allowed to observe for a year or two how this test will work out when applied to people from 65 to 69.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) said this morning that inasmuch as everyone has condemned the means test as applied to people 70 and over it would appear contradictory to recommend an eligibility test for people from 65 to 69. In other words, the opinion has been expressed that if the means test has been considered to punish thrift and prevent employment of people 70 and over, a somewhat similar eligibility test would have the same effect if applied to people from 65 to 70. To my mind that is far from being a foregone conclusion. The special committee expressed an opinion in that regard, and I should like to refer to paragraph 47 of the conclusions, which reads:
It may be doubted whether, in terms of priorities, the diversion of such a large extra amount of the national income to this particular group can be

justified, particularly when such a large proportion of the people in this age group are still actively engaged in productive employment and self-supporting. There is an advantage in universality when the large majority of the age group concerned is retired. That advantage does not obtain to the same extent when the majority of the age group concerned is still active and self-supporting.
It has been said that the application of a test to people from 65 to 69 would prevent the employment of people in that age group. On the contrary, it seems to me that the implementation of a universal system of pensions from age 65 could have the psychological effect at this time of leading the mass of the people to believe that no one should work after 65, and that the recognized universal retirement age should be 65. Nothing could be worse for the Canadian economy at this time and also for the citizens themselves from 65 to 69. Let us not forget that; and I quote from page 99 of the report:
Due to improved health services and the consequent increase in the longevity of our population, along with other factors, our aged population is growing from year to year. In 1931 the average life expectancy for new-born males was 60 years and for females 62 -1 years.
In 1947 the life expectancy of new-born males and females had risen to 65-18 years and 69-05 years respectively. I am convinced that the 1951 figures would be still higher. We have in 1951 approximately 1,100,000 people 65 and over. The report continues:
This trend towards an ageing population may reasonably be expected to continue through the decades ahead.
In Canada during a period such as the one we are in at the present time, a period of practically full employment, there are 5,300,000 people gainfully employed, which is a proportion of 4-8 gainfully employed people for each person 65 and over. If we accepted the age of 65 as the universal retirement age it would mean that five persons gainfully employed in Canada would have to contribute for the living of the sixth. In other words, if we had, as we have heard it advocated many times, a universal pension of $50 a month at age 65, which is even below what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) requested this morning, it would mean that each person gainfully employed in Canada at this time would have to contribute an average of $10 a month out of the national income for the purpose of old age security alone. I am not convinced that the people of Canada will be ready to go so far at this time. I should like to refer to page 101 of the report where it reads:
As large numbers of persons reach what may, under present circumstances, be considered the normal ages of retirement, and as they find themselves in better health, it may be expected that they will show increasing reluctance to accept the
Old Age Assistance Act inevitability of retirement at such ages. It is in the interests of the individuals themselves and of the country as a whole that we should re-think our attitude towards continued gainful occupation of these older age groups. The committee believes that increasing emphasis should be placed on efforts to remove from people's minds the idea that there is any set or accepted age for retirement. Each individual in the nation's population should be encouraged to continue as long as possible in gainful employment. Not only is this a matter of importance to individuals themselves in terms of their health and mental outlook, but it is of even greater importance to the over-all economy of the country. Surely a country like Canada, with a wealth of natural resources still in large part undeveloped, is justified in having profound faith in its economic future. If we are to develop these resources adequately, we shall need' to retain in active undertakings the largest possible number of our nation's population. The committee believes that, in the years ahead, our economic progress and prosperity will depend in significant measure on the success of efforts made to utilize to the fullest possible advantage the mature skills of these older workers.
It is my personal opinion that if at this time we had a universal pension at 65 it would have the psychological effect of having the mass of the people believe that the accepted retirement age in Canada was 65 years. As far as this is concerned I said in committee and I want to repeat here that personally I deplore the fact that the government itself is not setting a very good example in that regard.
I and the majority of Canadians who think as I do may be wrong, but, if we are, the situation which will be created under this bill can be corrected. If on the other hand the proposal for universal pensions at 65 was Implemented and it turned out that we were right in our apprehensions and those other hon. members who proposed it were wrong there would be no remedy, no way back.
That was the attitude I took in committee, and I believe it was reasonable. Those who held opposite views came to a reasonable compromise. I urge hon. members not to talk so much about things that may be done in future. Let us first try this system instead of making speeches so that two or three years from now one may say, "Oh, well, I was the first to advocate it in the House of Commons." I do not believe we should play politics with this question. This is a good bill; it is something the people of Canada want. I urge this house to approve the terms of the compromise reached in the committee. I am convinced that all hon. members will be only too happy to approve the principle of the bill which is the first step towards placing Canada in the forefront of the world as far as provision for old age security is concerned.

Old Age Assistance Act who has just taken his seat, I want to indicate how much we of the committee appreciated the work he did. It was not an easy task. We came to the committee with varying views. I think that joint committee on old age security was parliament at its best.
The importance of this bill does not arise from the amount of money involved but rather from its principle. In one stroke the recommendations of the committee now being implemented have brought about the beginning of a universal pension at 70, the beginning of the end of the means test, and the payment of pensions to a new group from 65 to 69. In my opinion this is a historic measure of social significance. Hearing the speeches made today endorsing the principle of the bill brought to my mind a military principle. In the presence of such distinguished soldiers as I see here I am a little hesitant about expressing it, but perhaps they will forgive me. I believe the first thing one is taught in the army is that when you have attained your immediate objective the next thing you do is consolidate your position to make sure no one takes it away from you. It seems to me we should give a little thought to that principle at this time. How much social security? Well, as much as the people want and are prepared to pay for. Where is the limit? I do not know. I do know we have not reached it yet.
We must recognize that this measure came about as the result of an overwhelming public clamour. They asked us to do away with the means test, and to lower the age limit. The government heard that demand and timed it-timing was important in this case-in such a way that it is now acceptable to all the people of Canada. I make that point not so much for the effect it may have on this and the other bill that will be introduced, but because there is still so much to do. The other day the question of national health insurance arose. There are many champions of national health insurance in this house, men who will be not only persistent but determined to bring it and keep it actively before the house. Unfortunately, the people have not yet clearly made their wishes known. Those same lobbies and interests that were advocating the removal of the means test and lowering of the age limit have not been heard from. I believe the people will make their wishes known on health insurance. They are also prepared to pay for it.
It is very difficult for me to follow this galaxy of speakers, who know the old age pension problem from A to Z and try to find something new to say.

The significance of that fact must not be lost. There has been a feeling in this house that for too long we have neglected these people. Because they have no great lobby, because in most instances their families look after them in their own way instead of making their plight public, their voices have not been heard. I wish to say a word or two in support of old age pensions. I have not done so for several years. There was a time when I spoke regularly in support of a better old age pension for our senior citizens of Canada, but I have more or less given myself over to other activities lately, and consequently have left this matter to other members in my group. However, I have not by any means lost my interest in this matter. I heartily support the bill which is now before the house. I should like to congratulate the minister who has, by long and strenuous efforts, finally been able to accomplish the objective he has for several years had in mind.
May I just say one word in respect to the matter of financing this measure? What the member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) has said requires serious thought. If we were to enter a depression we should have serious difficulty indeed raising the money to support such social services as we all desire to support. Even with our revenues as buoyant as they now are, I imagine the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has grave misgivings as to the ability of the nation to finance these ambitious plans which everyone desires to see materialize.
May I point out to the members once more what I laboured to point out to them on June 20? On that day I spoke about the Bradbury experiment in England during world war I. I believe that everybody who read the words I uttered on that occasion must have been impressed with the fact that a state-created unit of money was used with a great deal of success in Britain during that most trying experience of the war.
State money can be used for lending as it was in the Bradbury experiment. Surely similar state money could be used for spending to finance such things as old age pensions, pensions for the blind and pensions for the incurable. In the friendly discussion which I had with the Minister of Finance that night, it was brought out that sound money was money which was supported by sufficient goods and services and a stable price structure. The more goods and services that this


country can produce and put into the market, the more money can be put into circulation in the country. If sufficient goods and services can be fabricated and brought into the markets of the country, enough state money can be created to, shall we say, "chase those goods".
It is common in the house now to say that inflation results from too many dollars chasing too few goods. That is correct. If you get plenty of goods for the dollars to "chase", you will not have any trouble. If you get too many goods for the dollars to "chase", then prices will come down too far and you will have a depression. As the amount of goods for the dollars to "chase" increases, then the government could safely create and spend into circulation more dollars to "chase" those goods. I am using the common expressions which are used in the house.
That will be very encouraging to all who have to do with the matter of financing. That is the test. As our production overtakes our effective demand, as I believe it now has done in Canada, it is going to become more and more feasible for the government to create money debt free in this nation. That will mean a new source of revenue so that it will not be necessary to put upon the provinces the burden of financing old age pensions, pensions for the blind and all these other social services. The dominion government can assume that burden through its constitutional ability to create money debt free backed by the goods and services of the country.
I wish to point out to the minister that the next time the member for Macleod asks him that question of his, the minister can answer it just this way:	"With our wonderful
machines now coming into use, our wonderful technological skills, as a result of which we can make almost anything from almost anything-as for example nylon-and with the remarkable extent to which we can employ solar energy for the fabricating or processing of our resources into desirable goods, we have no fear in the world of being unable to finance the old age pension or any other social service we may consider it wise to finance. If we once adopt the understanding that the state can create money, independent of the banks, to represent the goods and services as they increase in the land, our only concern then is going to ibe to produce enough goods and services. Surely everyone in this house and in this country realizes that we can produce all the milk, cream, butter, cheese, apples, meat, coal and other things the people might need to enable them to enjoy a good standard of living. There is no question concerning that matter".

I would say this much just by way of encouraging the Minister of Finance, and to reassure the people of the country, that if we will adopt a sound, realistic financial system we simply do not need to be afraid to bring into being all the social services we desire.
A question has been raised as to whether we could safely create and spend much debt-free money at the present time in Canada. I cannot be sure about that. The stand I have taken all through this year has been that our supply position is good enough to permit that we create money even today, probably hundreds of millions of dollars of it, and spend it safely not only on old age pensions but in other desirable ways. If our supply position is not sufficient we would not be able to create new money without causing difficulties. But if our supply is adequate we would be able to create and spend new money safely. As to whether or not our supply is adequate, we would have to have the experts of the land study the whole question and then report to us.
I believe it would be interesting to hon. members to study the two important bank letters of June, namely, the Bank of Nova Scotia monthly letter and the Bank of Montreal monthly letter which have just come to our desks today. They speak rather glowingly of the tremendous increase in Canadian production, and point out that we are now in a rather sound supply position, and we are rapidly becoming more sound because, we might say, the productive capacity of the nation is completely overtaking the financial capacity of the nation to consume. If such be the case, and I believe it is, then the minister could arrange matters with his colleague, if he could bring him to see eye to eye with him, which must be done, to provide for the financing of a great many of these expenditures by the device of creating debt-free money backed by the goods and services in the state and capable of coming into existence in the state through the use of the resources both human and material in the state.

There was agreement among many provinces that provision should be made for income casually earned, but there was not unanimity on that. No one finally suggested an amount that was higher than what is contained in the present bill.
Many of the provinces did say that as this was a new departure we ought to build on experience and that while there were objections to the extent of the level of the permissible income that is now contained in the Old Age Pensions Act, experience ought to be allowed to develop before we made any fundamental change. Great reliance was placed upon the committee's report during our discussions.
While most of the provinces would have preferred to provide for the permissible income through casual earnings in regulations rather than in the act, the more we thought of it, and as a result of subsequent discussions over the telephone and so on, the clearer it became that to leave casual earnings to the extent of any stated increase permitted by way of regulation and not by statutory direction would create difficult if not almost impossible administrative problems for the provinces.
One province that had had great experience because of its huge population simply said that it would be impossible to administer a regulation covering a permissible income up to a certain amount. -I can only say that in the light of these discussions, although the decision was not made known to them at the
(Mr. Martin.]
time, we have decided that the most convenient way to increase the permissible income was in the act, and we have done that. May I point out that when the arrangement was made for other income of $20 for single persons and $30 for married persons, that recognized the preferential difference to which the minister has referred in favour of the single person. That was agreed to by the provinces and the minister made a great deal out of that in 1947. I remember very well when we debated the changes in the act on that occasion. Since the provinces agreed to that figure at that time I feel certain that if the government had taken the responsibility of making these figures such as to provide $20 of other income for single persons and $30 for married couples there would not have been any objection from any province. I repeat that the only reason we got into this situation of having the two figures identical was an accident, and my legal friend to my right reminded me last time I used that phrase that it was an accident and not an act of God.
I have in my hand a copy of the 1948 office consolidation of the Old Age Pensions Act. It has been metamorphosed into a 1950 office consolidation by making in it the only changes necessary to incorporate the amendments of 1949. That year all we did was to change two words; indeed we just changed one word twice. We changed "thirty" to "forty" in two different places. In other words, what was being done in 1949 when we increased the basic pension from $30 to $40 was to make the change just as simply as the government could possibly arrange it, and it was doing it in that simple way that produced the accident of making the allowable income for a single person and a married couple the same. During the debate on second reading there seemed to be some displeasure felt by hon. members on the government side of the house that some of us on this side did not confine


our speeches to praise of this bill. As a matter of fact, we did indicate, all of us who spoke, our real pleasure that this measure has been introduced. I need not go into that again. Maybe we said too much along that line. But I feel that hon. members who want us to be perfectly satisfied with it and do nothing but praise it, are not fully in touch with the times nor with what is taking place in the field of social security. I had occasion this morning to take up the minister's remark that the work of our special committee had been noted in the United States. Indeed, I quoted from a publication which I had received, put out by the Federal Reserve Bank in Chicago, dated September, 1950. It is entitled "Business Conditions". My quotations from this pamphlet this morning were in the field of theory regarding old age security.
I shall now take a moment to refer to an article in this same pamphlet entitled "Federal Old-Age Insurance Program Expanded." It is an account of the changes in United States social security legislation resulting from the approval of H. R. 6,000, which was passed on August 28, 1950. That refers to a bill which received approval in the house of representatives on that date. The article deals with improvements made in the old age security legislation in the United States, and I am keenly interested in discovering that there have been improvements made since our own special committee studied the situation in the United States last year. I am satisfied that our committee profited greatly by our study of United States experience. The place where we have shown that profit the most is by deciding on the principle of universality at least for those of age 70 and over.
Lest the minister get away with the statement that we have the finest program in the world, which is quite an exaggeration, let me point out that according to this article the changes made by H. R. 6,000 provide some real improvements in the amount of the old age payments made in the United States. I quote briefly from the article:
For workers retiring in the next few years, the changes are expected to raise the average benefits to $50-55, which is significantly above the average amount currently paid under old age assistance.
Then a little later in the same paragraph we find this:
Furthermore, the maximum total benefit payable, including special allowances, is increased from $85 per month to $150.
I submit that this morning when I was expressing dissatisfaction over the fact that we have provided a pension of only $40 per month, and when I was suggesting we should now be considering old age pensions of $60

per month, I was not being extravagant at all in relation to conditions on the North American continent. In the eyes of some the figure I was suggesting was still too low. I make that answer to those members who were not satisfied because we did not spend all our time praising this measure. It is a good measure, because it lowers the pensionable age to 65, and even though that is all it does we are glad we are getting it on the statute books. But this $40 with which we are starting off for the group from 65 to 69 is a figure that, before very long, we shall certainly have to increase, and I shall continue to urge that that be done.

the second reading of Bill No. 396, to provide for allowances for blind persons.

He said: Mr. Speaker, in view of the importance of this measure I believe I should make a brief statement in connection with the second reading. Apart from the large number of those now receiving pensions who will benefit from the more generous provisions of this measure, an additional 2,000 to 3,000 blind persons will for the first time receive benefits, either under this measure or under the old age security act. It is noteworthy that for the first time under this bill blind people of our country will have separate legislation of their own quite independent of that respecting our aged citizens. I think this bill will be welcomed by all who have urged the enactment of separate legislation for the blind and a different name for the benefits payable to them. On both counts the government has accepted the recommendations of the six-point program put forward in 1947 by the Canadian Council of the Blind, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind and other individuals and organizations working in this field.
Examination of their program shows that the government in this measure or otherwise is implementing, either wholly or in part, each of the recommendations made, as follows:
1.	Separate legislation is provided for the blind under the title recommended, "the Blind Persons Act."
2.	The term "pension for blind persons" has been abolished in favour of "blindness allowance."
3.	The amount of the blindness allowance is in accordance with that recommended in the six-point program of 1947.
4.	The residence qualification is drastically reduced.
5.	The income ceilings have been greatly liberalized.
6.	While not provided for in this bill, a good deal of progress has been made in recent years in making medical treatment available for the blind.
Under the bill presently before us we are now taking an important additional step in the further liberalization of the test of eligibility for the blindness allowance by raising the income ceilings by an additional $120 a year.
Income ceilings in this Blind Persons Act, as compared with those in effect prior to 1947, will be higher by the following amounts:

For a single person, raised from $500 to $840 $340

from $700 to $1,040	 340

Blind Persons Act
The payment of allowances to blind persons from 21 to 69 is, of course, a matter of joint federal-provincial concern. We have gone as far as any of the provinces expressed a desire to go at the federal-provincial conference on May 23 and 24 in the direction of liberalizing the test of eligibility to be applied under the Blind Persons Act. As I have said, a major forward step has been taken in reducing the residence requirement from 20 years in the existing act to 10 years in the new measure. This will make a significant number of persons eligible for these allowances who at present have insufficient residence.
For some years now we have included in our departmental estimates, under the blindness control division, an appropriation for the purpose of defraying 75 per cent of the cost of surgical expenses incurred in connection with eye operations on selected blind pensioners. A number of the provinces have taken advantage of this provision and have contributed 25 per cent of the surgical costs involved. In 50 per cent of the cases dealt with to date vision has been successfully restored and the pensioners have been able to give up their pension and return to normal life in the community. This, I believe, is very satisfactory progress. This program holds considerable promise for the future. We propose to continue and expand it to the extent that the provinces co-operate.
I may add also that a great deal has been done under the national health program to help combat the problem of blindness. Glaucoma clinics have been established in Toronto, Montreal and Quebec city, where research and treatment are being carried out. We look forward to satisfactory developments from this experiment which is being put forward by some of the provinces and acted upon in relation to the number I have indicated.
As members of the house are aware, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind does a great deal of work in the treatment, training and rehabilitation of the blind. In recognition of this, the government, a year or so ago, increased its grant to the institute from $18,000 to $45,000 and increased its grants to a number of other organizations carrying out similar functions.
We are pressing forward vigorously with new programs in this important field and urging upon the provinces that they should take the fullest possible advantage of funds available under the national health program to develop whatever additional undertakings commend themselves to the provincial health authorities.

Blind Persons Act
Most of the new features of the old age assistance legislation to which I have referred in an earlier debate are applicable also to the present legislation. Indians will henceforth be treated on exactly the same basis as other persons under this federal law and will be equally entitled to all its benefits.
Recoveries from estates will no longer be required under federal legislation. It will be left to each province to decide whether it wishes to continue this practice under provincial law. Under the new bill, in the event of a blind person's death, the allowance may be paid for the full month in which the recipient dies. In other respects as well, this legislation has been rearranged and brought up to date in conformity with the Old Age Assistance Act.
The house will have noted, I am sure, thax the two pieces of legislation parallel each other closely, many of the sections of both bills having almost identical wording. There are, however, three important points of difference between these measures, in addition to those which I have already mentioned.
Since we will be continuing to make payments under this new act to essentially the same persons who are now receiving blind pensions under the Old Age Pensions Act, and since the basis of sharing the present costs of blind pensions is 75 per cent federal and 25 per cent provincial, it has been considered advisable to make no alteration in this respect.
There is no provision in section 7 of this bill corresponding to section 7 (a) of the Old Age Assistance Act permitting the provinces to decide upon a different age of eligibility from that prescribed in the federal act or to lay down other special conditions of eligibility. Uniformity is essential in the Blind Persons Act so that nothing is done to jeopardize the rights of any persons now receiving blind pensions.
Section 13 of the bill is an important one. It is designed to ensure the continuation under all conceivable circumstances of the benefits of the present old age pensions legislation as they affect blind persons, regardless of any action that may or may not be taken by the provinces.
On November 30, 1950, the total number of blind persons in Canada was found to be 18,262. When account is taken of the coverage provided under the Blind Persons Act, the Old Age Assistance Act, the old age security act, the War-Veterans Allowance Act, the Pension Act for veterans, family allowances, the provincial workmen's compensation and mothers' allowance laws and other legislation, it will be found that the blind

population of Canada will be assisted to a degree and an extent not surpassed by any country in the world.
Of the 11,540 blind persons between 21 and 69 in November last, no fewer than 7,238 persons were in receipt of blind pensions under the Old Age Pensions Act. On January 1, 1952, they will be entitled to receive the extra benefits of the Blind Persons Act and will be covered by the more generous provisions of its modified eligibility test.
Then, in addition to this group, when the old age security act comes into effect on January 1 next approximately 6,000 blind persons aged 70 and over will automatically become eligible for the universal pension, free of the means test.
These two acts alone will provide next year benefits for almost 15,000 of the 19,000 blind persons in Canada.
Of the 4,302 blind individuals as of November 30 last who were not in receipt of pension under the Old Age Pensions Act, 276 were receiving war veterans blind pension; 187 were receiving benefits under workmen's compensation; and others were receiving assistance under mothers' allowances, family allowances and other measures.
Of the remainder, a certain number will now become eligible under the reduced ten years' residence clause. The others, for the most part, have means of their own, are engaged in full-time employment, or are the wives, husbands or relatives of sighted persons who are able to provide for themselves.
For fifteen years, since allowances for the blind were first introduced in 1936, they have occupied a relatively obscure but nevertheless important place in our Old Age Pensions Act. Now, for the first time, with the concurrence of this parliament, they can receive their proper recognition, with a status and standing of their own. Every Canadian can feel proud that through this measure he is doing something to help those of his fellow citizens who bear this heavy handicap.
In time we can hope that medical science will prevent more people from losing their sight. We can be confident that new drugs and new skills will be developed to lead others back from the unending night of blindness, but those Canadians who are now without the faculty of sight and those who will lose it in the years ahead will continue to command our warm admiration. They can be sure of our unfailing support.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES- PAYMENTS AT AGE 21
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to commend this bill, and I am sure that it will receive not only the unanimous, but the hearty support of all members of the house.

One is very glad indeed to see at last that provision for allowances for blind persons is being made in a statute separate and apart from the statute which provides allowances or pensions to persons by reason of old age. There are historical reasons why the two groups were included in the one act, the joint dominion-provincial scheme applicable to the two groups being similar. But the time has long since been reached when separate statutes should be set up to provide independently for the two groups, and the departures which are being taken at this session and in the fall session, in the light of the report of last year's special committee of both houses on old age security, have made this a most opportune time for the introduction of a separate bill dealing with allowances for blind persons.
The various points which the minister has mentioned in connection with the bill are, I think, in every case points that will receive endorsement on the part of members of the house. One is especially glad to see more generosity being displayed with respect to the supplemental income which persons are, under this act, entitled to receive before losing anything of the permissible allowance. The courage and the independence which so many persons who suffer from the handicap of blindness show day by day are a challenge to all of us who have the blessing of sight. 1 particularly like the feature of the bill which is going to raise the maximum limits of permissible supplemental income because those who have been leading the cause of our blind persons and seeking assistance for them in the kind of measure we have before us have at all times laid the greatest possible emphasis upon encouraging our blind citizens to help themselves.
I think the provision, as far as it goes, made for increasing the maxima of permissible income is in line with the efforts of those who have been seeking, both in parliament and outside, to educate the public in the most helpful way of bringing assistance to those who suffer this handicap. They do. not ask for charity, and they never have. They simply ask for understanding and a limited form of assistance which will enable them with their own efforts to make their own way in life. I think the emphasis which the minister has properly laid upon the increases in permissible income is entirely well directed and will commend itself to the judgment of the house.
Fifteen years have passed since the first measure of public assistance to blind persons on the part of the federal authority was inaugurated. The step that is in the process
Blind Persons Act
of being taken in this house tonight is altogether commendable, and an important step forward.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES- PAYMENTS AT AGE 21
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too want to say that the bill is a most welcome and acceptable one. The things that it does are highly desirable and I am sure will meet with the unanimous approval of the house. The main thing that it does of course is to put our legislation respecting the blind in a separate statute. In point of fact it does two or three other things that are of substance. It reduces the residence requirement in the case of the blind from twenty years, as it has been in the statute, to a period of ten years. It also, as with the Old Age Assistance Act that we dealt with earlier today, does away with recoveries from estates. I realize there is still the possibility for recoveries to be made if the provinces exercise that right, but the wording of the act would actually seem to discourage the provinces from pursuing that practice. It also slightly liberalizes the other income that blind persons are allowed to earn.
For all three of these points of substance I am sure there will be deep appreciation on the part of those interested in the welfare of the blind, as indeed it will be welcomed that we are now to have a separate statute for our blind persons. Having said that, I feel I cannot let what the minister said tonight go by without drawing attention to the way in which he sought to claim, at least by inference, more for the bill now before us than is actually to be effected by its terms.
The minister read off very quickly a list of figures comparing the income ceilings provided for in this bill with those respecting blind pensioners that were in effect prior to 1947. It is perfectly legitimate for the minister to put it in that way if he wishes to do so, but I think he should tell the whole story, and not try to give a wrong impression. He pointed out that prior to 1947 the ceiling for single blind persons was $500 and that this bill would make it $840, an increase of $340. He said that for a single blind person with dependents the ceiling prior to 1947 was $700 and that it will now be $1,040, an increase of $340. With respect to a married blind person living with a sighted spouse he said the income ceiling prior to 1947 was $925 and that it will now be $1,320, or an increase of $395. And he said that in the case of a married couple both blind the income ceiling prior to 1947 was $1,000 and that it will now be $1,440, an increase of $440.
Frankly, I was disappointed that the minister did not point out that he was

Blind, Persons Act
making a comparison with something that does not now obtain. At the present time the ceilings for these four categories are not the pre-1947 figures he gave. Rather, those ceilings are $720, $920, $1,200, and $1,320. Those income ceilings have been in effect since the act was amended in 1947. In other words the change in the other allowable income being provided by the bill now before us is only $120 in each case, and I object strongly to the minister suggesting that the legislation now being presented to parliament makes increases in other allowable income as substantial as those he placed upon Hansard. The actual increase for each category is only $120. As the minister was describing the various benefits provided under the act he referred to this as the modified eligibility test. You do not change the means test to something else simply by changing its name. It is true that the means test has been slightly relaxed in the case of blind people as in the case of those coming under old age assistance, but only to the extent of $10 a month. I welcome that change; I am glad we have that relaxation in the means test; but let us not try to kidi ourselves or anybody else into thinking we have got rid of the means test because we call it a modified eligibility test.
I was a little startled also at the way the minister sought to suggest that all the things to be done for our blind persons after this bill passes are the result of this bill. It makes quite a picture when the minister lines up the assistance provided under the War Veterans Allowance Act, under the Pension Act, under the Family Allowances Act, under the compensation laws of the provinces and all the rest of it. But though it is quite a picture it is certainly unfair- indeed it is misleading-to suggest that all this is being done by the bill now before us.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES- PAYMENTS AT AGE 21
speechtext:
All the applause the Liberals may give that statement will not alter the fact that the minister placed on the record a set of figures which left the impression that much larger increases in other allowable income were now being effected than is actually the case under this bill. As I said a moment ago I heartily welcome having our. blind legislation in a separate statute, and I heartily welcome the three changes of substance set out in this bill. But let the government not try to claim that more than this is being done at this time. They can take credit if it means anything to them for what has been done in the past, for what has been done by provincial governments and by other organizations, including private groups working for the blind. But let the minister be fair in presenting a bill like this and claim for it only what it actually does.
There is something not in this bill, and I say quite frankly I am sorry it is not here. I realize that this legislation has come about as a consequence of the changes that have been made in the old age pension legislation. In view of those changes; in view of the federal government paying 100 per cent of the pensions to those 70 and over; in view of the government undertaking to pay 50 per cent of the pensions to those 65 to 69; it was necessary to have a separate act for the blind in order to continue the 75-25 relationship, and also because blind persons receive their allowances starting at the age of 21.
In spite of all that, however, this bill deals with little but the three changes in substance to which I have just referred. It does not deal with a very important matter that is of great concern to the blind. I believe Canadians from coast to coast would agree that the least our modern society should do for these people would be to give them this allowance without any means test at all. The minister referred to the various requests of the blind organizations which had been met, some of them rather small such as changing the name of the pension to an allowance and putting their legislation in a separate statute. He said nothing, for example, about the request of the Canadian federation of the blind in a letter addressed to him on June 20 of this year, copies of which I take it have been

sent to all members of parliament, that the means test be abolished altogether as far as the blind are concerned. The very figures the minister gave tonight as to the assistance blind persons get under several different statutes, showing that a very large proportion of our blind persons qualify for assistance of one kind or another, make clear how simple and relatively inexpensive it would be to go the whole way and give all our blind persons 21 years and up, since that is the age now in the statute, the blindness allowance free of a means test.
I was interested, as I am sure other hon. members were, in an editorial on this matter in Thursday's issue of the Ottawa Citizen, in which the writer estimated that it would cost only a little more than $3 million annually in addition to what we are now spending to do this for these people who live their lives, as the minister said, in the blackness of a long night. I am satisfied any Canadian you could approach would say we should do that, and I hope the day is not far distant when we will go that further step and provide this blindness allowance completely free of any means test.

speechtext:
I am not going to make any extended remarks on this bill, Mr. Speaker, because if I said what was on my mind I would simply repeat what I said this afternoon on the other bill. This bill is an improvement and will be welcomed. It may not be all that we would like to see brought in for the blind, but it is at least a step in the right direction. We favour it. I shall just repeat this to reinforce the arguments I put forward this afternoon concerning the incurables in Canada. The blind can be classed as incurable, and therefore in respect to the blind this is a commendable piece of legislation. Now, how about the others who are incurable, but who perhaps are not blind. They may be just as unfortunate in other respects as those who are blind. I hope and trust that the day is not far distant when other incurables are written into some such act as this.
There is a difference between the two types of incurables. We do have the blind. It is a very unfortunate position for them to be in. While they may be blind, they may otherwise be very healthy people. You may have, on the other hand, incurables who have their sight but they may be bedridden. They may be wheel chair patients. From a financial point of view they may be in a far more serious position than some of the blind, yet there is no legislation covering them. I am not making a comparison between the two unfortunate classes of people. I suppose if
Blind Persons Act
most of us had our choice as to whether to be a wheel chair case or blind, we would prefer to be a wheel chair case. Perhaps there is nothing more unfortunate than blindness. The legislation is commendable and we are not going to criticize it. It is an improvement, but I do hope and trust that some action will be taken in respect of legislation for other incurables.

The provision as to the extent of blindness is covered by regulation 28. The regulation states:

Mr. Chairman, we have very little opportunity in the House of Commons to talk about the federal district commission, and the work being carried on by that body and the national capital planning committee. I think it is unfortunate indeed that there is not more opportunity, because I think members as a whole are not familiar with the work being carried on in Ottawa and the adjoining district.
I would make the suggestion now that once every four or five years the officers of the federal district commission should come before either the committee on banking and commerce, the public accounts committee or some other body, and explain the work being carried on by the commission, so that hon. members may be informed in more detail as to future plans to be carried out.
This bill contains only a few amendments to be incorporated in the act. However, it stands as another example of a series of amendments to an act that I suggest should be revised, because this is the sixth time since 1927 the Federal District Commission Act has

been amended. It is clear that over a number of those years the work of the commission has changed. New plans have been proposed and new burdens placed on the shoulders of those who administer the act.
From time to time the commission has found that it did not have the powers necessary to carry out the duties given to it. In the present instance we are dealing with railways. However, I believe there will be a question connected with the industrial area. As hon. members know, the federal district commission has acquired huge tracts of land for the specific purposes of the act, mainly for parks, roadways and similar facilities around the Ottawa area. However, owing to the recommendations of the national capital planning committee, it is now necessary to consider certain arrangements which have been made with the railways, the city and the municipalities as to the provision of industrial and railway sites. To carry out these duties the federal district commission is finding from time to time that it has not the power to do certain things.
Although by virtue of the provisions of the Expropriation Act the commission has power to buy lands and to expropriate lands for park purposes, it did not have powers for certain other purposes. I understand the commission has had to resort to the device of having the Department of Public Works expropriate certain lands, which in turn will be turned over to the federal district commission for its purposes. This was done because the federal district commission could not acquire or purchase lands for railway and industrial sites. That is an unfortunate situation.
I think all hon. members would be anxious that the commission should have the proper powers to carry out the responsibilities given by parliament. I for one will welcome the day when this act is completely revised.
I should like to say a few words about the acquisition of land. I have had some experience in the operation of the Expropriation Act in acquiring lands for the Department of Public Works and for the federal district commission, and my experience leads me to believe that the Expropriation Act is another act which requires revision. It is an old one, having been used in the exchequer court and the supreme court for years and years. Judgments from those courts have been turned over from court to court, to the point where, although I do not say the Expropriation Act does not give justice, I feel it does not give to the party whose property is being expropriated just what parliament through its legislators would have given, had the circumstances been known.

In present circumstances, when properties are expropriated the law as it was set out in the Expropriation Act is rigidly applied. In this district the homes built along the Ottawa river and the Rideau river have been suddenly expropriated, and the order has been given for their removal. Up to the moment they have not been removed. I must add that the owners have been treated kindly; the terms with respect to their remaining in their homes have been fair, and the officers have been as considerate as they could be; but they are continually threatened by the provisions of the Expropriation Act in so far as the prices they are ultimately to be paid for their properties are concerned.
Under that act there is nothing to be given to these persons, in the sense that the average person would expect. The Expropriation Act says that the value to be given is the actual value of the property at the time of expropriation. All of a sudden a person who built his house fifteen years ago finds that it is to be expropriated, and feels that there is injustice in the fact that he must accept the so-called actual value, and at the same time have to move four or five miles outside Ottawa where there are no local improvements, no water and no sewers. These people are confronted with the necessity of having to build houses which will cost twice as much as they paid for the houses being expropriated. The person in question is not paid anything for displacement. Value is placed on nothing but the actual market value of the house as it stands.
In many cases this is a hardship. The difficulty does not lie with the officers of the federal district commission, or in any suggestion that they have been unfair in their treatment of the people concerned. On the contrary they have left those people where they were in most places, with the promise that they may remain for five years. But the problem would arise in five years' time as to where they shall go. By that time new homes will cost much more than they get through the exchequer court. Furthermore the owner of a house worth $12,000 cannot afford to go to the exchequer court. I just want to bring this matter to the attention of the committee and through the committee to the attention of the Prime Minister, as I have done before. I think it is time that some revision was made in the method of settlement for expropriation proceedings in order that the hundreds and hundreds of people who are faced with these proceedings may be treated more fairly.
The membership of the federal district commission is rather large today and the commission is kept quite busy. Certain rela-
Federal District Commission Act tionships must exist between the federal district commission and the municipalities that compose the national capital area. There should be some body to act as a liaison. I should like to end these few remarks by saying that we in this district have the greatest appreciation of the fine work being done by the federal district commission.

Mr. Chairman, as one who comes from the upper reaches of our great Canada may I say just a word at this time. As a youth I happened to be in Ottawa when Sir Wilfrid Laurier proposed to build here the Washington of the north. I am amazed that in the interval there have been allowed to be created conditions which make this capital of our great country a place of confusion rather than a place where our aspirations and hopes and ideals can be joined in harmony.
Coming as I do from a more remote area of Canada, I want to see here a city beautiful, a city such as was envisaged by Mackenzie King in his day. I like to wake up in the morning with thoughts of the Peace river country, of the Fraser valley, of the Okanagan or the valleys of Nova Scotia, but I find that I wake up in the morning filled with nausea because of the sulphurous miasma from Hull. That is much against the interest of good government in this country.
We have sulphide mills and paper mills, but they should have their place. Each of us has his place. God does not create any person or any object that does not have a proper place. It is a bad thing to take a sulphurous mess like that and project it into the heart of the government of Canada. I knew the late E. B. Eddy who founded the industry over here. In his day he did great work as we are now doing up in the Peace river and elsewhere. But time marches on, and as time marches on these places should take their proper places with respect to the great objectives of the nation.
I was up at Kingsmere the other day with the hon. member for Yukon-Mackenzie River to pay a tribute at that little cottage where Mr. Mackenzie King lived for so many years. Some of us are rich, some of us are poor, but we all looked upon Mr. Mackenzie King as a great statesman, a man of great heart, and of course power and opportunity. We went out to Kingsmere and saw the humble cottage in which he lived, where he dreamed his dreams and where he wrote out his scheme for Canada. The hon. member and I drove back to Ottawa and as we approached the city we could see the spires of the churches and the towers of the parliament buildings. It looked like a city beautiful, it looked like something that would inspire.

Federal District Commission Act
I said to the hon. member that that was something that should make for peace and good will among men. But then we turned here and we turned there, we went this way and we went that way; we went through the confusion and through the mess which man had created. Instead of coming to the great spires of a city beautiful when we did get to Ottawa and pulled up in front of the Chateau Laurier we were met with complete confusion. I defy any man in this House of Commons, whether he be a member of the C.C.F., the Social Credit, the Liberal or the Conservative party, to go across that street at right angles.
Some of us here are trappers, some are miners, some are farmers and some are bankers, but we all come to what should be a city beautiful and find it to be a city of great confusion. Is it not time for us to pause and think a while? I have been a reader of the Ottawa Evening Journal for many years and I know that they have their ideas, their hopes and their aspirations. I think it would be a good thing for this House of Commons to make plans in order that this capital of Canada may be a city where ideals can be mingled regardless of our religion or our race, whether we come from the east or the west.
A great city should be built around the Commons of Canada so that people in generations to come will say, "Those people builded well."

In 1944 a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons was set up to look into this question. At that time they recommended a rearrangement of railway facilities which was carried into the general plan with respect to which I tabled a report in this house some time ago and of which a model is now on display in the lobby. The plan required the removal of certain trackage which comes right into the city, the presence of which has much to do with the confusion in front of the Chateau Laurier to which the hon. member for Cariboo referred a few moments ago.
The federal district commission set up this national capital planning board with a railway subcommittee. Officials of the two railways using the Union station are members of that subcommittee; and with the full co-operation of all those concerned a satisfactory arrangement was worked out under which the federal district commission would acquire an area in Ottawa South and construct trackage facilities on it; then when it was ready, under this agreement the Canadian National Railways would cede to the federal district commission the trackage it was abandoning in the heart of the city and would use that being provided in Ottawa South. It is to give the federal district commission such powers as are necessary under


the Railway Act to carry out that undertaking that this clause has been drawn. The hon. member will see that anything which has to be done under the clause has to get the approval of the board of transport commissioners. It has to comply with the ordinary requirements of the Railway Act in carrying out these powers.
On February 12 I filed the report of the federal district commission for 1950, in which there is a description of what has been done up to the present time. The act requires the commission to file a report each year showing what is being done. It may be desirable at some time-certainly the government would have no objection-to have this report referred to the public accounts committee or to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, or to a select committee, where the officers of the commission could be called as witnesses to familiarize members of the committee and of parliament with what is being done under the act.
I think there is very effective control by parliament over what the commission does, because for each of the last four years parliament has been appropriating into a special fund an amount of $2,500,000, of which most is still unexpended, for carrying out this work by the federal district commission. The members of that commission serve without remuneration in order to be of service to their fellow citizens. Certainly they are very sensitive to any views expressed by parliament as to the proper way for them to earn the gratitude of their fellow Canadians by this devoted service they are performing for the community. It amounts to about $1.50 a ton on the shipment of western grain and was a reduction in the' receipts of the railways. Our' western people have been rather surprised and disappointed at having received a notification from the railways very recently that they were going to cancel C.F.A. tariff item 145, and the only reason they gave is:	"Conditions which
prompted the establishment of those rates in 1933 do not obtain today."
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is my belief that this loss of C.F.A. 145 would be absorbed in the federal freight assistance. I think that is correct, at least that is the information that has been given me, but that if C.F.A. were ever dropped then the rates on these grains westbound would be up $1.50 a ton.
I want to compliment the minister on this policy across the years of making western feed grains available to farmers in other parts of Canada. It has made a permanent imprint on agriculture in Canada, and I think it has been sound policy for agriculture in the western provinces as well as for the production of livestock and livestock products in the western province of British Columbia, and also the eastern provinces. It is a splendid policy and I hope it will be continued. I draw to the minister's attention the notice given to western receivers of the cancellation of C.F.A. 145.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That was only a short time ago. We did consider the whole matter at that time and we decided it was not something we should carry on from Ottawa. It is being done provincially. The types of fertilizers used in different places across Canada are quite different. For instance there are certain large areas where this particular type is not used at all. For that reason it was looked upon as something that more properly could be carried on in the different provinces, in accordance with their needs.

But at the present time you are subsidizing lime which is used only in certain areas. I understand most of it is used in the maritime provinces. I have no objection to that; indeed I think it is a good idea, and it is carried out in many countries. The subsidization of fertilizers is done in most agricultural countries, as a matter of fact. I should think that when the government is subsidizing lime in certain areas it should give consideration to subsidizing the use of fertilizers in other areas, so that there would be a similar policy across the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Where lime is used in considerable quantities it is usually on the least productive of our lands. That is the only reason for providing assistance from the central government as well as the provincial governments, where that condition prevails. We have not thought it advisable to go into other lines in this country. I realize there are other countries where they have only a central government, and where it does all that kind of thing. But in a federated country like Canada we think it is better for the provincial government to take care of matters of this kind in accordance with the needs of the area, rather than that we should take care of it.

Supply - Agriculture
informed by them that the regulations are occasioned by the danger of typhoid carriers and that sort of thing. speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not know that it was necessary to come back to this item to discuss this matter because it really has not anything to do with the item. The regulation is really a health regulation, and it is a matter which was dealt with quite recently in order to make it more binding than it was before. The reason for that was a typhoid epidemic in the province of Alberta in which several people lost their lives, and it was traced back to cheese which had not been properly matured. That is the claim that was made long before pasteurization was known of at all, that if you made cheese from milk and properly cured it you were then safeguarded against anything of that kind being in the cheese. It has been proven quite recently that there were some people who contracted typhoid from the use of cheese which had not been properly cured. The health regulations make it necessary to mature it for ninety days before selling it. That is what the regulation is. I could not say we would undertake to have it changed.
